what_it_does: Tiny wireless sensors — think a sensor on a bridge or in a field — often run entirely on harvested ambient energy (solar, vibration, radio waves) rather than batteries. These devices capture data at a steady rate but can only process it as fast as the environment supplies power, which fluctuates constantly. When the gap between capture rate and processing rate opens up, the device's small input buffer (a fixed-size queue of unprocessed readings) fills up and overflows, permanently losing sensor events. Quetzal is a combined hardware circuit and software runtime that closes this gap: a small power-measurement circuit provides real-time energy readings to a scheduler, which picks the next processing job by minimizing total time including the time it will take to recharge enough energy for future jobs. Before committing to a job, a mathematical queuing model predicts whether the buffer will overflow before the job finishes; if so, the runtime automatically reduces the job's workload (lower quality, shorter duration) to speed up processing and drain the queue.
